candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk II.4 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Cyril carefully defends Christ's address to His mother at Cana ('Woman, what have I to do with thee?') against any reading that would imply disrespect. 'Woman' (gynai) is for Cyril a formal address of honor, not familiarity-refused; the question is rhetorical, situating the miracle within His Father's appointed timing rather than maternal pressure. Mary's authority remains intact (she immediately directs the servants to obey Christ) — the verse establishes the principle that Christ's miracles proceed from the Father's will, not human request, even when that human is His own mother. Tewahedo Marian veneration preserves this delicate balance.

'Fill the waterpots with water' Cyril reads as the typological pivot of the entire Cana sign: Christ deliberately requires human cooperation (the servants' labor of filling) before the divine transformation. The six stone waterpots — used for Jewish purification rites — Cyril reads as the six days of creation (the imperfect order awaiting completion), or as the Old Covenant's purification economy awaiting Christ's New Covenant fulfillment. The water-to-wine transformation prefigures the eucharistic transformation: the elements remain (water/bread), but their inner reality is changed by Christ's word.

'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up' is for Cyril a Christological saying of central importance: the temple in question is not Herod's structure but Christ's body, and the active agent of the Resurrection is the Son Himself ('I will raise it up' — egerō auton). Against subordinationist readings that would make the Resurrection a passive event done TO Christ by the Father, Cyril insists on the Son's active agency: the Word raises His own assumed humanity through the divine power that is His own by nature. This is the dogmatic root of the Tewahedo Easter Anaphora's doxology of the Risen Christ as agent of His own resurrection.

John's interpretive aside — 'He spake of the temple of His body' — provides Cyril his exegetical warrant for body-as-temple typology that runs throughout his John commentary. The Old Covenant temple (with its court of Gentiles, holy place, holy of holies) prefigures the structure of the incarnate Christ: His flesh is the new court where Gentiles enter, His soul the new holy place, His divinity the new holy of holies indwelt by the Father.
